stories.title: Ethiopia: Red Cross Warns of Worsening Humanitarian Crisis in Oromia
stories.summary: Ethiopia: Red Cross Cautions of Worsening Humanitarian Crisis in Oromia As Conflict, Displacement Deepen Civilian Hardship Addis Standard Internally displaced people from the Oromo community in western Oromia shelter in Adama, Ganda Saqaqalloo area, receive community support at a mosque (file photo) 19 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has warned that the humanitarian situation in Ethiopia's Oromia region is deteriorating amid persistent armed conflict, deadly civilian attacks and growing displacement, saying it is struggling to reach all communities affected by the escalating insecurity. The organization said on Thursday that communities across several zones of Oromia were enduring severe hardship as fighting and insecurity continued to disrupt their lives. The ICRC, working alongside the Ethiopian Red Cross Society (ERCS), said it had intensified humanitarian assistance in conflict-affected areas, particularly in western and southern Oromia, over recent weeks. Oromia has been grappling with a protracted armed conflict involving federal forces and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) since 2019, alongside increasingly fragmented security crises, intercommunal violence and clashes along regional boundaries. The deteriorating security situation has also been accompanied by growing public grievances over local governance, alleged coercive practices and economic disruption.

An environmental justice activist has warned that proposals to expand carbon dioxide removal technologies under consideration at the COP31 climate negotiations could threaten African livelihoods, worsen food insecurity and divert scarce climate resources from adaptation projects. Kwami Kpondzo, an official of the Global Forest Coalition and co-coordinator of the Africa Working Group of the Hands Off Mother Earth (HOME) Alliance, said large-scale deployment of technologies such as bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) and marine carbon dioxide removal could impose significant costs on communities already vulnerable to climate change. In an interview with PREMIUM TIMES in Antalya, Türkiye, Mr Kpondzo argued that the growing emphasis on carbon removal risks allowing major polluters to continue emitting greenhouse gases instead of reducing pollution at its source. stories.title: Tanzania: Tanzania Re-Elected to Influence Global ICT Policies
stories.summary: Tanzania Re-Elected to Influence Global ICT Policies 19 November 2026 Tanzania Daily News (Dar es Salaam) Doha — TANZANIA'S re-election to the Council of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) gives the country another four years to influence global telecommunications policies, with implications for affordable internet access, digital inclusion, cybersecurity and the future of technology in developing countries. Securing 131 votes in elections held on Monday, during the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference (PP-26) in Doha, Qatar, Tanzania will serve on the 48-member Council for the 2027-2030 term, strengthening its opportunity to contribute to international decisions affecting the development of the global Information and Communication Technology (ICT) sector. The victory gives Tanzania a platform to advance issues that directly affect its digital transformation ambitions, particularly expanding affordable connectivity, improving access to digital services, strengthening cybersecurity and ensuring developing countries have a meaningful voice in shaping emerging technologies. For Tanzania, the significance of the renewed mandate will ultimately be measured by how effectively it uses its position to influence international policies and cooperation in ways that support domestic digital development. Of the 48 Council seats, 13 are allocated to Region D (Africa), with Tanzania securing one of the positions.

stories.title: Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bududa has suffered repeated deadly landslides over the years By Ondiro Oganga Â and Â Swaibu Ibrahim ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Kampala Published 19 November 2026, 09:04 GMT Updated 5 hours ago Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations. The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides. Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods. The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.

stories.summary: Malawi: Three in Four Malawians Drinking Contaminated Water, Shock Survey Finds Nyasa Times Women drawing water. 19 November 2026 Nyasa Times (Leeds) By Zawadi Chilunga Nearly three in four Malawians are drinking water contaminated with faecal matter, even though most households say they use improved water sources, according to a National Statistical Office (NSO) survey. The NSO found faecal contamination in the drinking water of 74.6 per cent of the population when it was tested in the household, compared with 35 per cent when it was tested at the source. Its report says contamination rises sharply between the water source and the home, pointing to transport, handling and storage as the weak points. The findings are alarming because 91.2 per cent of households use improved sources such as boreholes, protected wells and piped taps. stories.title: Zimbabwe: Constitutional Court Reserves Judgment in Challenges to Mnangagwa's Term Extension
stories.summary: Zimbabwe: Constitutional Court Reserves Judgment in Challenges to Mnangagwa's Term Extension ED Mnangagwa/X President Emmerson Mnangagwa. 18 November 2026 New Zimbabwe (London) The Constitutional Court on Wednesday reserved judgment in two challenges to constitutional amendments extending President Emmerson Mnangagwa's rule to 2030. This comes after lawyers had argued that the entire legislation should be struck down over alleged procedural violations in Parliament and that the extensions should not benefit the incumbent president and MPs. Constitutional lawyer Lovemore Madhuku, representing the applicants, said the court had heard arguments challenging the insertion of ten provisions into the Constitutional Amendment Bill that were not included in the original gazetted proposals. He said the applicants wanted the entire Constitutional Amendment Act No.3 invalidated if the court found that the provisions had been introduced without following the constitutionally prescribed procedure. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "Our arguments were intended to show that they had not complied with the requirements in Section 328(3), which would not allow Parliament to proceed to deal with any constitutional provision that was not part of the case stated in the notice," Madhuku told journalists outside court. "We were arguing in that paper that if they agree with us that the 10 provisions were not supposed to be in the Bill because they had not been consulted on them, then they must set aside the entire Act. "Madhuku said selectively removing the disputed provisions through what lawyers call the "blue-pencil test" would fundamentally change the legislation approved by Parliament, potentially undermining the basis on which lawmakers voted for it. "We argued that if they were to do so, the Bill would be different from what it was when Parliament passed it.

stories.summary: Burkina Faso Targets Critics in Exile Â© RFI 18 November 2026 Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC) By Ilaria Allegrozzi Junta's Arrest Warrants, Extradition Requests Extend Crackdown Abroad Journalists, activists and political opponents who fled Burkina Faso to escape the junta's repression now risk arrest and prosecution abroad, as the country's judicial authorities pursue dozens of individuals over alleged terrorism-related offenses. Burkina Faso Prosecutor General Désiré Sawadogo announced on November 13 that a special court handling terrorism-related offenses had opened six cases against at least 45 people and entities. All those targeted exposed serious military abuses during counterinsurgency operations and include exiled journalists critical of the junta, among them Ahmed Newton Barry , Issaka Lingani , Inoussa Ouédraogo , Adama Ouedraogo, and Abdoulaye Barry; exiled social media activist Naïm Touré ; former foreign affairs minister Alpha Barry , and international journalist Wassim Nasr . They face various charges, including complicity in terrorist associations and financing terrorism. Burkina Faso sent international arrest warrants and extradition requests to Côte d'Ivoire, France, and the United States, said Sawadogo.

The Northern State Humanitarian Aid Commission says it has secured an exceptional allocation from the WFP after food supplies to the camp were interrupted. stories.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Strain-Specific Ebola Vaccines to Be Trialled in DR Congo, WHO Announces
stories.summary: Congo-Kinshasa: Strain-Specific Ebola Vaccines to Be Trialled in DR Congo, WHO Announces WHO A participant in the eastern DR Congo receives a vaccine as part of a trial to tackle the Ebola Bundibugyo virus. 18 November 2026 Radio France Internationale By RFI Two vaccines against the deadly Bundibugyo Ebola strain gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo are set to enter trials in the outbreak's epicentre next week, the World Health Organization announced on Tuesday. "We expect two candidate vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo virus to begin testing as early as next week," World Health Organization (WHO) chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told a press conference at the United Nations health agency's headquarters in Geneva on Tuesday. The so-called Tumaini trial in the Democratic Republic of Congo ( DRC ) will test the safety, efficacy and ability to trigger an immune response. The trial uses the ring vaccination method of immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Ervebo, a vaccine already approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, kicked off the Tumaini trial on 23 October, at the full-scale Phase 3 level, to determine if it also offers any protection against Bundibugyo. There are currently no vaccines or treatments for the less common Bundibugyo species of Ebola , which is responsible for the outbreak declared in May that triggered an international public health emergency.

stories.title: Sénégal: au moins un mort et des dizaines de disparus dans un nouveau naufrage de migrants
stories.summary: Sénégal: au moins un mort et des dizaines de disparus dans un nouveau naufrage de migrants Au Sénégal, un nouveau naufrage d'une pirogue avec à bord des personnes voulant émigrer vers l'Espagne a fait au moins un mort et plusieurs dizaines de disparus. Survenu au large de Yenne, une ville côtière à une quarantaine de kilomètres au sud de la capitale, dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi, le drame n'a fait qu'un seul rescapé retrouvé pour le moment. Les recherches des gendarmes et des pompiers se poursuivaient mercredi 18 novembre 2026 dans l'après-midi. Publié le : 19/11/2026 - 04:25 3 min Temps de lecture Au moins un migrant a péri dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi au large d'une commune de pêcheurs de l'ouest du Sénégal, après le naufrage d'une pirogue transportant des dizaines de personnes, selon les autorités locales et les secours (image d'illustrartion). © AFP Par : RFI avec AFP Publicité Lire la suite Il était environ 2 heures du matin lorsque la pirogue a heurté des rochers au large de Yenne, selon le maire de la commune, Massamba Mbengue, et un responsable politique local, Mamadou Ndione. « On pouvait entendre les cris provenant de la pirogue, audibles même depuis la plage », raconte Oumar Sow, représentant du chef du village. Un corps a été repêché après le drame, d'après le maire et les pompiers.

stories.title: Madagascar: ouverture du procès du drame d'Ambohimalaza qui fit une trentaine de morts en 2025
stories.summary: Madagascar: ouverture du procès du drame d'Ambohimalaza qui fit une trentaine de morts en 2025 C'est un drame qui a bouleversé Madagascar et ébranlé le pouvoir en juin 2025 : plus de 30 personnes, pour la plupart des jeunes, mouraient après avoir mangé lors d'une fête d'anniversaire près d'Antananarivo. Empoisonnement aux plantes, botulisme : les versions se sont succédé, sans jamais convaincre les familles. Mercredi 18 novembre 2026, le procès s'est enfin ouvert. Et durant cette première journée, un médecin a livré des informations contredisant les précédentes explications. Publié le : 19/11/2026 - 04:25 3 min Temps de lecture Vue générale d’une salle d’audience à Antananarivo, à Madagascar, le 8 octobre 2015 (image d'illustration) AFP - RIJASOLO Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Avec notre correspondante à Antananarivo , Aurélie Kouman Dans la salle d' audience , les familles des victimes du drame d'Ambohimalaza étaient suspendues aux lèvres du professeur Pierre Rasolonirina, mercredi 18 novembre, au premier jour de ce procès très attendu à Madagascar.

stories.title: Soudan: le chef des paramilitaires FSR de nouveau condamné à mort par contumace
stories.summary: Soudan: le chef des paramilitaires FSR de nouveau condamné à mort par contumace Au Soudan, le tribunal antiterroriste de Port-Soudan a condamné par contumace à la peine capitale, ce mercredi 18 novembre, le chef des Forces de soutien rapide (FSR), Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, dit Hemetti, ainsi que ses deux frères, Abdelrahim et Al-Kouni, et onze autres commandants. Au total, quatorze accusés ont été condamnés. Le tribunal a également ordonné aux condamnés de verser d'importantes indemnités, s'élevant à 40 milliards de dollars, soit environ 36,5 milliards d'euros.

stories.title: Sahara occidental: Washington réaffirme son engagement après l'annonce de la fin de la Minurso
stories.summary: Sahara occidental: Washington réaffirme son engagement après l'annonce de la fin de la Minurso Moins de trois semaines après l'officialisation de la liquidation de la Mission des Nations unies pour l'organisation d'un référendum au Sahara occidental (Minurso), l'ambassadeur américain à l'ONU, Mike Waltz, s'est rendu mardi 17 novembre 2026 au Maroc pour prendre part à plusieurs entretiens stratégiques liés au dossier du Sahara occidental. Tête-à-tête avec le chef de la diplomatie marocaine, la cheffe du gouvernement et l'ancien patron de la Minurso : Mike Waltz est venu réaffirmer la position américaine. Publié le : 19/11/2026 - 04:24 2 min Temps de lecture Le ministre des Affaires étrangères marocain Nasser Bourita (à droite) avec l'ambassadeur américain auprès de l'ONU Mike Waltz (àa gauche) à Rabat le 17 novembre 2026. © AP Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Les États-Unis resteront impliqués dans la résolution du conflit au Sahara occidental . Alors que le camouflet au Conseil de sécurité de l' ONU et le veto russe sur le projet de réforme de Washington laissaient présager un retrait du gouvernement Trump, l'ambassadeur américain Mike Waltz a confirmé que la résolution rapide de ce dossier reste une priorité. « Les États-Unis vont continuer de travailler avec toutes les parties et avec l'ONU. Comme l'a dit le président Trump, le statu quo est inacceptable.

stories.title: Afrique du Sud: le nouvel ambassadeur du Nigeria rappelé à l'ordre sur fond de violences xénophobes
stories.summary: Afrique du Sud: le nouvel ambassadeur du Nigeria rappelé à l'ordre sur fond de violences xénophobes À peine arrivé, le nouvel ambassadeur du Nigeria en Afrique du Sud est déjà rappelé à l’ordre par Pretoria. Femi Fani-Kayode a accusé les autorités sud-africaines d’avoir volontairement coupé la retransmission de son discours lors de la remise de ses lettres de créance au président Cyril Ramaphosa. Un simple « problème technique », répond le porte-parole du président. S’ensuivent des échanges tendus sur les réseaux sociaux, puis une convocation du diplomate, sur fond de tensions entre les deux pays liées notamment à la vague de xénophobie qui touche la nation arc-en-ciel, à laquelle le nouvel ambassadeur a promis de s’attaquer. Publié le : 19/11/2026 - 04:24 2 min Temps de lecture Le nouvel ambassadeur du Nigeria en Afrique du Sud, Femi Fani-Kayode (au centre à gauche), aux côtés de responsables du Congrès des progressistes (APC), à l’issue d’une conférence de presse à Abuja, au Nigeria, le 27 février 2023 (image d'illustration). © Ben Curtis/AP Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Avec notre correspondant à Johannesburg, Valentin Hugues « Nous avons versé de notre sang durant vos heures les plus sombres », déclare le nouvel ambassadeur du Nigeria face à Cyril Ramaphosa , avant de refuser une interview à une chaîne publique sud-africaine et de justifier son choix sur son compte X.

stories.title: Rétrocession des Chagos à Maurice: Port-Louis exige d'être associé aux discussions entre Londres et Washington
stories.summary: Rétrocession des Chagos à Maurice: Port-Louis exige d'être associé aux discussions entre Londres et Washington Maurice hausse le ton sur le dossier des Chagos. Le Premier ministre mauricien, Navin Ramgoolam, exige que son pays soit pleinement associé à toute discussion entre Londres et Washington sur l'avenir de la base militaire anglo-américaine de Diego Garcia, la principale île de l'archipel des Chagos. Actuellement sous administration britannique, les Chagos font l'objet d'un accord prévoyant leur restitution à Maurice. Mais sa mise en œuvre reste bloquée, notamment en raison de désaccords entre Britanniques et Américains sur le sort de leur base militaire. C'est sur ce sujet que Maurice entend être consultée.

stories.title: Libye: le chef du renseignement égyptien à Tripoli pour renforcer la coopération avec le gouvernement Dbeibah
stories.summary: Libye: le chef du renseignement égyptien à Tripoli pour renforcer la coopération avec le gouvernement Dbeibah Le chef des renseignements généraux égyptiens, Hassan Rachad, était en début de semaine à Tripoli, en Libye, où il a rencontré le Premier ministre du gouvernement intérimaire, Abdel Hamid Dbeibah. stories.title: Peine de mort en Afrique : du Nigeria au Burkina Faso, le continent face aux revirements
stories.summary: Peine de mort en Afrique : du Nigeria au Burkina Faso, le continent face aux revirements En vingt ans, le nombre de pays africains abolitionnistes a doublé. Mais, par ailleurs, le Burkina Faso vient de rétablir la peine capitale et des dizaines d’autres États la maintiennent sans l’appliquer. stories.title: Africa: Climate Finance Needs Proof, not Promises
stories.summary: Africa: Climate Finance Needs Proof, not Promises 18 November 2026 allAfrica.com opinion By Smith Nwokocha In Gidan Dare, a farming community near the BUA Cement plant in northwest Nigeria, residents describe wells that once reached water at three or four metres now requiring seventy or more metres before anyone strikes anything. They describe their mud houses cracking and collapsing under the vibration of heavy truck traffic. They talk about how, close to midnight, plant operations are loud enough to disturb their sleep. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) says it confirmed “broad community support” for the expansion during a site visit in August 2022. Yet none of the community leaders I spoke with recall being consulted before BUA expanded onto land their families had farmed for generations.

stories.title: Central African Republic: Rights Defender in Central African Republic Dies
stories.summary: Central African Republic: Rights Defender in Central African Republic Dies 18 November 2026 Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC) press release By Lewis Mudge Remembering Nicolas Tiangaye, Who Fought for Constitutional Safeguards Until the End Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70. One of the country's most respected rule of law advocates, his career spanned more than four decades. Tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986. Later he defended the future president, François Bozizé, when he was accused of plotting a coup. For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by.

stories.title: Nigeria: Jigawa Farmers-Herders Clash Leaves Three Dead, Two Injured
stories.summary: Nigeria: Jigawa Farmers-Herders Clash Leaves Three Dead, Two Injured 18 November 2026 Vanguard (Lagos) By Muhammad Inuwa, Dutse At least three people have been killed and two others injured in a violent clash involving suspected herders and farmers in Garki Local Government Area of Jigawa State. The incident reportedly occurred at about 3:30 a.m. on Wednesday at Wauta Fulani Settlement in Rafin Marke Ward, Kanya District. The statement said efforts by farmers to prevent further destruction of their crops reportedly triggered an attack by the suspected herders, who allegedly wielded cutlasses, bows and arrows.

stories.summary: Mines : la stratégie XXL de la Côte d’Ivoire pour devenir le prochain eldorado africain La Côte d’Ivoire veut faire des mines et de l’énergie le deuxième pilier de son économie. stories.title: Egypt: CPJ Urges Congress to Raise Press Freedom Violations With Egypt Foreign Minister
stories.summary: Egypt: CPJ Urges Congress to Raise Press Freedom Violations With Egypt Foreign Minister Abdel Fattah Al-Sissi/ Page Facebook President Abdel Fattah Al-Sissi 18 November 2026 Committee to Protect Journalists (New York) On Tuesday, the Committee to Protect Journalists sent a letter to members of the U.S. Congress, urging lawmakers to raise Egypt's unprecedented decline in press freedom during Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty's visit to Washington, D.C. this week. stories.title: Axes and cutlasses: Violence on Nigeria's election campaign trail
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5Pa3H Prefer DW on Google There are growing concerns over rising political violence ahead of the January 16, 2027 election Image: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Samuel Adebanjo had gone to the Oregun area of Lagos, the economic heartbeat of Nigeria , to cover a town hall meeting organized by the opposition party, the National Democratic Congress (NDC). But what was supposed to be a routine reporting assignment took a violent turn when a group of armed men stormed the venue and disrupted the gathering. "I was at the entrance, taking photos of people entering the hall when some buses drove in and I heard a loud bang," Samuel recalled. Before he could process what was happening, the men began chasing supporters of the party with axes, cutlasses, and wooden planks, forcing many to flee for safety. stories.title: Africa: The African Development Bank Group and JICA Explore New Avenues of Cooperation for Africa
stories.summary: The African Development Bank Group and JICA Explore New Avenues of Cooperation for Africa 17 November 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) The African Development Bank Group (Bank Group) and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) are looking to broaden their partnership in support of Africa's development, following talks between their leaders on 13 November. During an in-depth review ('deep dive') at JICA's headquarters, Bank Group President Dr Sidi Ould Tah and JICA President Dr Akihiko Tanaka first took stock of their cooperation across various sectors including agriculture and infrastructure, and then discussed new areas of opportunity. The two leaders were accompanied by their respective technical teams. Critical minerals, health, skills development, digital technology, artificial intelligence, resilience and crisis response were among the areas under consideration, alongside initiatives aimed at mobilising more private capital for Africa. Dr Ould Tah was keen to emphasise the potential of the partnership between the Bank Group and JICA to mobilise more private capital, promote access to technology and strengthen the engagement of Japanese businesses and investors in Africa.

stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The move comes amid persistent security crises across Nigeria, including banditry, mass kidnappings and communal violence By Basillioh Rukanga Published 18 November 2026 Nigeria has moved a step closer to introducing state police system after all 36 states approved a motion to create and operate their own police force alongside federal police. The resolution, which seeks to amend the constitution, now requires President Bola Tinubu's assent to become law. It also requires further federal and state legislation for state police to become operational. The move comes amid persistent security crises across Nigeria, including banditry, mass kidnappings and communal violence, which the federal security forces have struggled to contain. But critics fear that governors could use the forces to intimidate political opponents, suppress dissent or influence elections.

stories.title: Entre le FC Barcelone et Kinshasa, l’impitoyable match des intermédiaires
stories.summary: Le partenariat entre le club de football catalan et la RDC devait promouvoir la destination congolaise. Il a déclenché une guerre entre deux apporteurs d’affaires français, Aurélien Logeais et Olivier Nsiabamfumu, qui se disputent plusieurs millions d’euros.

stories.title: Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito By Akisa Wandera BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Lobito Published 18 November 2026 As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments. She is thinking about getting around more easily. The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast. For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient. "Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.

stories.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
stories.summary: Ursula von der Leyen and Abdel Fatah al-Sisi after a meeting in Cairo in March 2024. Photograph: Stavros Ioannides/PIO/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Ursula von der Leyen and Abdel Fatah al-Sisi after a meeting in Cairo in March 2024. Photograph: Stavros Ioannides/PIO/AFP/Getty Images European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi. The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen , the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

stories.title: En RDC, Ebola tue massivement les enfants : « Je ne peux même pas le prendre dans mes bras pour le réconforter »
stories.summary: Près des trois quarts des moins de 5 ans contaminés par la maladie à virus Ebola n’y survivent pas. A Bunia et Beni, épicentres de l’épidémie, les deuils s’enchaînent, tandis que plus de 2 280 enfants se retrouvent orphelins.

stories.title: Africa: An African Institution Will Not Be Put On Trial By Anonymous Sources and Politically Motivated Journalists

stories.title: Congo Ebola Outbreak: How Fear and Mistrust Drive Community Spread
stories.summary: As the Ebola virus spreads in eastern Congo, health teams struggle to curb fatal delays in seeking medical care and the widespread desire to treat sick relatives at home.

stories.title: Côte d’Ivoire : Blaise Lasm, Tidjane Thiam, Assalé Tiémoko… Le marathon judiciaire de l’opposition
stories.summary: Ce mois, nombre d’opposants sont attendus à la barre à Abidjan. Cinq ans de prison ont ainsi été requis ce 16 novembre contre Blaise Lasm, haut cadre du parti de Laurent Gbagbo. Tidjane Thiam doit également être fixé sur son sort ce 19 novembre. Voici les principales échéances à retenir.

stories.title: Faut-il oublier le projet de monnaie unique africaine ?
stories.summary: Plusieurs gouverneurs de banques centrales africaines jugent prématurée la création d’une monnaie commune sur le continent. Réunis à Luanda lors de l’AFIS, ils ont préconisé d’interconnecter d’abord les systèmes de paiement existants.

stories.title: L’arrêt très attendu de la Cour internationale de justice sur la question du génocide des Rohingya
stories.summary: La CIJ dira, jeudi 19 novembre, si la Birmanie a commis un génocide contre la minorité musulmane. Alors que la décision devrait préciser les contours de la définition juridique de « génocide », les tentatives d’intimidation américaines contre les juges se multiplient.

stories.title: Ecobank, Steinhoff, Nakumatt… Avant Nvidia, ces scandales africains qui ont provoqué la chute du CEO
stories.summary: L’éviction du patron de Nvidia rappelle la vulnérabilité des entreprises face aux dirigeants omnipotents. De Steinhoff à Ecobank, retour sur ces crises africaines nées d’un manque de contrôle du pouvoir exécutif.

stories.title: Comment Abdelmadjid Tebboune a rejeté la dernière tentative de rapprochement d’Emmanuel Macron
stories.summary: Afin de sécuriser les relations franco-algériennes avant la présidentielle de 2027, Paris a dépêché un émissaire à Alger. Qui s’est heurté au refus d’Abdelmadjid Tebboune de réengager le dialogue.

stories.title: Fresh clashes at the Eritrean border — is Ethiopia sliding into a regional war?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PXwP Prefer DW on Google Tensions in the Horn of Africa are at an all-time high Image: EDUARDO SOTERAS/AFP/Getty Images Advertisement After a few weeks of relative stability , fresh clashes in the contested Ethiopia-Eritrea border area have raised fears of a full-fledged war. Meanwhile, diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Sudan have hit new lows. Fighters allied with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched their offensive on September 23 . It was aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian government as part of a larger rebel coalition. But the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), backed by pro-government militia, have steadily pushed the TPLF out of Tigray, a region in northern Ethiopia .

stories.title: De Fela Kuti à Burna Boy, les radios de « GTA » racontent l’ascension des musiques nigérianes et sud-africaines
stories.summary: Dix-huit ans après avoir glissé des titres du père de l’afrobeat, le Nigérian Fela Kuti, dans le jeu vidéo « Grand Theft Auto IV », « GTA VI », qui sort jeudi 19 novembre, confie au chanteur nigérian Burna Boy une station entière consacrée aux musiques du Nigeria, d’Afrique du Sud et du Ghana.

stories.title: Avec Aliko Dangote, le Ghana peut-il relever son pari de la transformation locale du cacao ?

Le milliardaire nigérian projette d’entrer sur le marché du cacao au Ghana via un contrat de 500 000 tonnes. stories.summary: La spécialiste des mobilités et du droit des réfugiés décrypte, dans un entretien au « Monde », les logiques à l’œuvre derrière l’accord passé, lundi 16 novembre à Vienne, entre cinq pays européens et le Rwanda, permettant de renvoyer dans ce pays des demandeurs d’asile déboutés.

stories.title: COP31 en Turquie : cinq questions pour comprendre ce que peut en espérer l’Afrique
stories.summary: Alors que les pays africains réclament davantage de financements pour s’adapter au changement climatique, la COP31 se déroule dans un contexte international défavorable. Certaines priorités du continent sont néanmoins débattues.

stories.title: Comment les Africains ont sauvé la tête de l’OIF
stories.summary: Menacée de paralysie lors de son XXe sommet, l’OIF a échappé au blocage grâce à une « troisième voie » africaine. Plongée dans un marathon diplomatique sous haute tension au cours duquel Paris et les bailleurs ont été mis en échec.

stories.title: Le Togolais Gilbert Houngbo réélu à la tête de l’OIT
stories.summary: Le Togolais Gilbert Houngbo a été reconduit à la tête de l’Organisation internationale du travail. Il entend placer l’intelligence artificielle au cœur des enjeux de justice sociale.

stories.title: Chaos as crackdown on illegal mining in Guinea causes wave of regional displacement
stories.summary: Artisanal gold miners in Kanadjiguilla, Mali, clamber on to a repatriation vehicle bound for Burkina Faso. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Artisanal gold miners in Kanadjiguilla, Mali, clamber on to a repatriation vehicle bound for Burkina Faso. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Chaos as crackdown on illegal mining in Guinea causes wave of regional displacement Ban on illegal artisanal mining triggers mass exodus and diplomatic tensions with neighbouring Sahel states In the border town of Kourémalé, split between Guinea and Mali, thousands of families have been trudging across the frontier over the past week after a sudden ban on illegal artisanal mining triggered a wave of displacement and a regional diplomatic dispute. Some, like Seydou Traore, a miner in his 30s from Burkina Faso , made the 78-mile trek from Kourémalé to Ouezzindougou, farther inward. Last week, he gathered a small bundle of his belongings and fled Guinea after security forces ordered him and fellow miners to leave. “We worked hard there, honestly,” he told Agence France-Presse (AFP). “Then one day everything changed.

stories.title: Pourquoi MTN veut s’offrir l’intégralité de Telkom, et pas seulement sa fibre
stories.summary: MTN revient à la charge pour acquérir 100 % du capital de son concurrent Telkom SA. Malgré de probables contraintes réglementaires, le projet permettrait à l’opérateur de devancer Vodacom en nombre d’abonnés mobiles.

stories.title: Sahara occidental : combien de soldats et quelles armes possède réellement le Front Polisario ?
stories.summary: Après son appel à la mobilisation générale du 10 novembre, le Front Polisario affiche sa détermination face au Maroc. Mais de quels moyens militaires dispose réellement le mouvement indépendantiste sahraoui ? Effectifs, blindés, artillerie, soutien algérien : radiographie d’une armée à l’arsenal vieillissant.

stories.title: Génocide des Tutsi : devant la cour d’assises de Paris, le procès du Rwandais Madjaliwa Safari et des tueries aux « barrières »
stories.summary: Arrêté à Tours en 2023, le commerçant de 61 ans est poursuivi pour les faits imprescriptibles de « génocide » et de « crimes contre l’humanité ». D’après plusieurs témoins, il aurait ordonné des meurtres et participé à des massacres de Tutsi en 1994.

stories.title: ‘I’m not ready to go to jail’: co-founder of Egypt’s last independent media outlet faces prison
stories.summary: Lina Attalah, editor in chief of the Cairo-based Mada Masr, will be in court this week on charges of ‘publishing false news’. Photograph: K Desouki/AFP/Getty View image in fullscreen Lina Attalah, editor in chief of the Cairo-based Mada Masr, will be in court this week on charges of ‘publishing false news’. Photograph: K Desouki/AFP/Getty ‘I’m not ready to go to jail’: co-founder of Egypt’s last independent media outlet faces prison Mada Masr, the news site co-founded by Lina Attalah just before the 2013 military coup, is fighting for its life after being shut down, but its journalists have not given up hope F acing a year in prison for running Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr , Lina Attalah is trying to focus on the everyday: waking at dawn to hear the birds sing before Cairo’s streets come alive and visiting Mada Masr’s shuttered offices with her reporters to water the plants and feed their four cats. Attalah is the reluctant face of Egypt’s embattled independent press at a moment of crisis. In the last six weeks, Egyptian authorities have waged a renewed crackdown on the few remaining independent media outlets left in the country, beginning with the arrest of the entire newsroom of the factchecking website Matsadaash.

stories.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
stories.summary: The Danish PM, Mette Frederiksen (centre), Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker (second left), and Rwandan minister Vincent Biruta (right) in Vienna on Monday. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters View image in fullscreen The Danish PM, Mette Frederiksen (centre), Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker (second left), and Rwandan minister Vincent Biruta (right) in Vienna on Monday. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”. The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country. In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

stories.title: BBC launches programme for children forced from school by bandits and poverty in West Africa
stories.summary: Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBC Image caption, Hadiza left school at 13 to get married and now spends her time doing housework By Madina Maishanu BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Goronyo Published 17 November 2026 As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school. "Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says. One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village. "They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says. Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home.

stories.title: Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda

stories.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
stories.summary: A debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger. Photograph: Nic Bothma/Reuters View image in fullscreen A debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger. Photograph: Nic Bothma/Reuters Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city. ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys Read more The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved. The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result.

stories.title: ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters
stories.summary: Beatrice Maseko, front, packs freshly harvested nyika tubers into a sack on the Shire riverbank, where water levels have reached highs not seen in decades. All photographs by Kenneth Zindondo View image in fullscreen Beatrice Maseko, front, packs freshly harvested nyika tubers into a sack on the Shire riverbank, where water levels have reached highs not seen in decades. All photographs by Kenneth Zindondo ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles T he mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika .

stories.title: Francophonie: le Rwanda accuse la France de pressions après le report de l'élection à la tête de l'OIF
stories.summary: Francophonie: le Rwanda accuse la France de pressions après le report de l'élection à la tête de l'OIF Le sommet de la Francophonie jette un froid sur les relations franco-rwandaises. L'Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) est si divisée qu'elle ne parvient pas à désigner un nouveau secrétaire général. Une première historique, mais aussi un revers diplomatique pour Kigali, qui souhaitait voir Louise Mushikiwabo rempiler pour un troisième mandat, sans se douter que la République démocratique du Congo (RDC), pays francophone le plus peuplé du monde, pèserait de tout son poids dans les discussions. Publié le : 19/11/2026 - 04:24 1 min Temps de lecture Au lendemain du report d’un an de l’élection à la tête de l’OIF, le ministre des Affaires étrangères du Rwanda, Olivier Nduhungirehe, s’en est pris à Paris dans les colonnes du Point Afrique : « L’OIF n’est pas la Françafrique ! » (image d'illustration). © RFI Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Kigali tient la France pour responsable de cet échec et l'a fait savoir par la voix de son ministre des Affaires étrangères, quitte à froisser Paris. « L'OIF n'est pas la Françafrique », a déclaré le chef de la diplomatie rwandaise dans les colonnes du journal Le Point , après avoir affirmé sur RFI que « la France a mis la pression aux pays africains ». Si Paris n'a pas officiellement réagi, cette offensive médiatique rwandaise fait grincer des dents jusqu'au sommet de l'État.

stories.title: Town rebuilt after devastating floods becomes showcase for Libyan strongman's rule
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Whole areas of Derna have been entirely rebuilt By Tim Whewell Reporting from Derna Published 16 November 2026 "It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna. Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him. Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya. It is part of a rapid $2bn (Â£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.

stories.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
stories.summary: Image source, Braton Serge/BBC By Ruth Alonga BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Butembo Published 15 November 2026 When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified. They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there. "Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him. But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive. This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern.

stories.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PRq5 Prefer DW on Google Nigeria's 2027 general election will take place against the backdrop of AI-driven disinformation Image: Adekunle Ajayi/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis . He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi. The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI) . Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died. The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election.

stories.title: Why Aid Isn’t Reaching Ebola’s Epicenter
stories.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has a new epicenter, one largely isolated from aid by an armed group that has killed and kidnapped aid workers. stories.title: Terror from the skies: drones are redefining warfare in Sudan, and massacring its civilians
stories.summary: View image in fullscreen Terror from the skies: drones are redefining warfare in Sudan, and massacring its civilians Composite: Guardian Design / Getty Images Strikes with huge death tolls are an increasing occurrence as UAVs ‘bring the war to places that were once safe’ The first drone struck the busy transport hub near a market in Al-Dibab as hundreds of people gathered to board trucks to take them back to their homes. Ten minutes later on the evening of 18 October, a second drone hit the same site in the town in West Kordofan state, Sudan . At least 139 people were killed. Eight days after the “double-tap” attack – designed to maximise casualties by killing and injuring emergency responders, volunteers and bystanders on top of the original victims – a drone hit a busy market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur. Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence in Sudan, put the death toll from that attack at 103. “I lost my 19-year-old son,” a Nyala resident told Agence France-Presse. “We buried him alongside more than 70 bodies in a single site.” View image in fullscreen The remains of Alneam market after a drone strike in the disputed Abyei region along the border between South Sudan and Sudan last month.

stories.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
stories.summary: By Victoria Gill Science correspondent In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass. Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him. More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary â but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

stories.title: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
stories.summary: Image source, Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF) Image caption, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba has signalled his intention to run for president in the next elections By Wycliffe Muia Published 14 November 2026 In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief. Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks. The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades. Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party. This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.

stories.title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: acrobatic Lagos producer Azzi on the Beat
stories.summary: Little room to catch your breath … Azzi on the Beat. Photograph: Yemi Osokaya View image in fullscreen Little room to catch your breath … Azzi on the Beat. stories.title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pro-government forces marched into Tigray's capital less than two weeks after the war began By Michael Teferi ,Â BBC Africa Â and Â Yemane Nagish ,Â BBC Tigrinya Published 13 November 2026 Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment. "People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC. After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter. "Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion. Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next." Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.
